---
title: "Staggered adoption"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment  = "#>",
  message  = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4,
  dpi = 96
)
```

```{r setup}
library(coresynth)
```

When units adopt treatment at different times, coresynth groups them into
adoption **cohorts** and aggregates the cohort ATTs with weights proportional
to `N_treated × T_post` (Clarke et al. 2024):

$$\hat\tau = \frac{\sum_g N_{tr,g}\, T_{post,g}\, \hat\tau_g}{\sum_g N_{tr,g}\, T_{post,g}}.$$

All six estimators support this; staggered timing is **detected automatically**
from the treatment column — no extra flag is needed.

The cohort ATTs themselves come about in two different ways. `scm`, `sdid`,
`gsc`, and `si` fit each cohort separately, against a donor pool you choose
with `control_group`. `mc` and `tasc` instead impute the counterfactual from a
single fit: their observation mask already blanks each treated unit from its
own adoption date, so one factorisation covers every cohort at once. That is
why those two take no `control_group` argument — all cohorts share the same
donor set, namely every observed cell in the panel.

## A staggered panel

Here `u1` is treated from period 11 and `u2` from period 16.

```{r dgp}
set.seed(42)
N <- 12; TT <- 20
f   <- cumsum(rnorm(TT, 0, 0.5))
lam <- rnorm(N, 1, 0.3)
dat <- expand.grid(time = seq_len(TT), id = paste0("u", seq_len(N)))
dat$y <- as.vector(outer(f, lam)) + rnorm(nrow(dat), 0, 0.3)

dat$d <- 0L
dat$d[dat$id == "u1" & dat$time > 10] <- 1L
dat$d[dat$id == "u2" & dat$time > 15] <- 1L
dat$y[dat$d == 1] <- dat$y[dat$d == 1] + 2.0   # true ATT = 2.0
```

## Fitting

```{r fit}
fit <- scm_fit(y ~ d | id + time, data = dat, method = "sdid")
fit$estimate          # aggregate ATT
fit$staggered         # TRUE
```

Per-cohort detail is in `cohort_estimates`:

```{r cohorts}
fit$cohort_estimates
```

## Choosing the control group

`control_group` controls which units serve as donors for each cohort in the
estimators that refit cohort by cohort (`"scm"`, `"sdid"`, `"gsc"`, `"si"`):

- `"never_treated"` (default) — never-treated units only.
- `"clean"` (deprecated) — never-treated units **plus** units adopting later
  than the current cohort.

Each cohort's effect is averaged over every period from its adoption date to
the end of the panel. A unit that adopts later is untreated before its own
date but treated after it, so under `"clean"` its **post-adoption** outcomes
enter the earlier cohort's synthetic control and pull the effect towards
zero. Neither source design does this: Clarke et al. (2024, Algorithm 1) use
pure controls only, and Ben-Michael, Feller & Rothstein (2022) admit a donor
only if it is untreated through the last event time they estimate. `"clean"`
therefore warns and will be removed in the next major release.

A staggered panel needs at least two never-treated units for these
estimators. When every unit is eventually treated, `"mc"` and `"tasc"` still
apply: they impute each unit's counterfactual from the untreated cells of the
whole panel rather than from a donor pool.

## Across estimators

The same call works for every method:

```{r all-methods}
methods <- c("scm", "sdid", "gsc", "mc", "tasc", "si")
sapply(methods, function(m)
  scm_fit(y ~ d | id + time, data = dat, method = m)$estimate)
```

## SCM: partially pooled synthetic controls

The classic SCM was designed for a **single** treated unit, so its staggered
extension rests on Ben-Michael, Feller & Rothstein (2022, JRSS-B). Units
adopting at the same time are averaged into one cohort — fully pooling within
a cohort is justified by their theory — and each cohort gets its own synthetic
control. How the cohort fits interact is controlled by `nu`:

- `nu = "auto"` (default) — the paper's heuristic, based on how well separate
  synthetic controls already balance the average.
- `nu` in `[0, 1]` — **partially pooled SCM**: all cohort weight vectors are
  chosen jointly, trading off per-cohort pre-treatment fit (`nu = 0`) against
  the fit of the *average* placebo gap across cohorts (`nu = 1`), which
  anchors the aggregate ATT. The paper advises against both extremes.
- `nu = "separate"` — each cohort fitted independently with the classic
  V-optimised SCM. This is `nu = 0` reached through a path that keeps the
  V optimisation, donor filtering and penalty options the pooled solver has no
  room for, and it is what the default falls back to when
  `donor_mspe_threshold`, `lambda_pen` or `v_selection = "oos"` is set.

`fixedeff = TRUE` (also the default) demeans every unit by its own
pre-treatment mean within each cohort (an intercept shift), which the paper
reports dominates the alternatives when outcome levels differ across units.

```{r scm-pooled}
fit_pp <- scm_fit(y ~ d | id + time, data = dat, method = "scm")
fit_pp$estimate
fit_pp$pooling[c("nu", "q_sep", "q_pool", "q_sep_separate", "q_pool_separate")]
```

`q_pool` (the pooled imbalance) improves relative to the separate solution at
the cost of a small increase in `q_sep` (the average per-cohort imbalance).
`scm_balance_frontier()` traces that trade-off across a grid of `nu`, which
the paper calls "an important tool for using partially pooled SCM in
practice".

Two further arguments control what the fit is aimed at:

- `pool_cohorts = FALSE` gives every treated unit its own weight vector (the
  paper's Section 4 formulation) instead of one per cohort (its Appendix A.2
  hierarchy, the default). `scm_rank_pval()` needs the unit-level form.
- `weights` sets the mass each treated unit carries in the aggregate ATT —
  a population or GDP figure, say, following Abadie (2021, S.8). It sets the
  block's target series, its weight in the pooled objective, and its
  aggregation weight alike.

### Auxiliary covariates

`covariates` partials the covariates out of the outcome before fitting, which
is the device SDID uses (Clarke et al. 2024, S.2.2). SCM has another option:
Ben-Michael, Feller & Rothstein (2022, S.5.2) *balance* the covariates
alongside the lagged outcomes, adding a second imbalance measure to the
objective weighted against the first by `xi`.

```{r scm-cov-balance, eval=FALSE}
scm_fit(y ~ d | id + time, data = dat, method = "scm",
        covariates = c("x1", "x2"), cov_method = "balance")
```

Each covariate enters as its average over the periods before the earliest
adoption, standardised on the donor units. `xi` defaults to the paper's rule,
the sample variance of those units' outcomes before the last adoption date;
raising it buys covariate balance at the cost of outcome balance, and letting
it fall to zero recovers the fit without covariates. The balance term needs
the partially pooled solver, so it cannot be combined with `nu = "separate"`,
`donor_mspe_threshold`, `lambda_pen` or `v_selection = "oos"`.
`fit$pooling` then also reports `q_cov_sep` and `q_cov_pool`, and
`scm_balance_frontier()` carries both across the `nu` grid. Read those
diagnostics differently from the outcomes-only ones above: the paper's
footnote 7 normalises by the *combined* measure, so `q_sep_separate` and
`q_pool_separate` are not the outcome imbalance of the `nu = 0` solution, the
`_rel` columns of the frontier are not 1 there, and the outcome imbalances can
both fall with `nu` because the covariate side is the third quantity being
traded off.

## Inference under staggered adoption

`sdid_inference()`, `gsc_inference()`, and `si_inference()` all extend to
staggered fits. `jackknife_global` is the staggered-specific variant that
removes each unique control unit across **all** cohorts at once, correctly
capturing cross-cohort correlation.

```{r stag-inf}
library(broom)
tidy(sdid_inference(fit, method = "bootstrap", n_boot = 100, seed = 1))
tidy(sdid_inference(fit, method = "jackknife_global"))
```

Staggered **SCM** fits use `scm_inference()`. Its default is the
leave-one-unit-out jackknife of Ben-Michael, Feller & Rothstein (2022,
Appendix A.1): each unit of the panel, donors included, is dropped in turn
and the weights refitted with `nu` held fixed, so the interval reflects the
noise in the synthetic controls as well as in the treated units.
`method = "wild_bootstrap"` gives their multiplier bootstrap instead, after
Otsu & Rai (2017): the weights stay fixed and every unit's term -- a treated
unit's effect, a donor's residual -- is perturbed by its own multiplier. It
needs no refitting, so it suits panels too large for the jackknife, and is
somewhat conservative.

```{r scm-inf, warning=FALSE}
tidy(scm_inference(fit_pp))
```

## Notes

- `plot()` and `augment()` for staggered fits operate per cohort; the aggregate
  synthetic series is not defined (`Y_synth = NULL`).
- SCM staggered adoption supports `covariates =` (partial-out) but not the
  `predictors = pred(...)` interface.
- SI additionally supports staggered **and** multi-arm simultaneously — see
  [Estimators](estimators.html#multi-arm-si).
